questions.question: should I treat my boots out of box ? Annnnd how often should I treat them ?

hybrid.answer:
**Out of the box:** it depends on the boot, and I've only covered Blundstones. Per Blundstone's FAQ, most of their boots come pretreated, so they don't recommend treating those out of the box [1]. The exception is rustic brown, Crazy Horse and rustic black leathers, which are distressed and don't carry the same pretreatment [1]. I recommend conditioning those, and I don't recommend leaving them dry [2]. Leather you've left unconditioned for a few months should be conditioned too [2]. Untreated or old leather that needs retreating isn't hydrophobic, so it dries out, cracks and breaks apart [3]. I haven't covered other brands or leathers.

**How often:** I don't have a fixed schedule. I do it when I feel they need it, and I personally probably do too little [4]. It depends on how much you wear them and where you go. Treat them if the leather looks or feels dry, or if water has stopped beading on top. Clean them regularly too, because dirt wears leather down faster [5].

I used to put it more strictly: once the pretreatment is gone you have to keep them treated, maybe monthly, or even weekly if you're hard on your boots [3]. Now I'd go by how the leather looks and feels.

questions.question: So if I buy the levis 501 shrink to fit will they get tighter after washing?

hybrid.answer:
Yes, the first soak and dry shrinks them, but they loosen again as you wear them. My advice is to size up so the shrunk fit works for you.

**Sizing up:** For Shrink-to-Fit 501s I'd usually go two sizes up [1]. They're sanforized-free denim that shrinks when you put them in the bathtub, so the size you buy won't be the size you end up with [1].

**How much they shrink:** The shrinking mostly happens as they dry [2]. When I tried mine on after drying, they had definitely shrunk, especially in the waist [3]. The length barely changed [4].

**Water and dryer:** Heat decides how tight they get. If you put them in the dryer, they'd start out a lot smaller [5]. I didn't use very hot water and I didn't use the dryer, and they looked way better [6]. So I'd avoid the dryer and very hot water for a nicer fit [6].

**After wearing them:** After a week the waist and thighs had stretched enough that I could wear a belt [7]. With frequent wear, I bet they stretch out to about the same size as regular rinsed 501s [8]. After about a year, mine fit really well [9].

**What I haven't covered:** I haven't said whether ordinary washes after that first soak keep shrinking them.

questions.question: I'm usually a 33x30 in Levi's 502s, what size should I buy in these? [501 STF]

hybrid.answer:
I'd go for a 35 waist and a 32 length. My rule for the 501 STF is to size up two in the waist and two inches in the length [1]. Applied to your 33x30, that gives 35x32. I haven't covered how the 502 fits compared with the 501, so I can't say whether your 502 size carries over in any other way.

**Why two sizes up in the waist**
- I still recommend going two sizes up on the shrink-to-fit 501 [2].
- The waist measures the same as a rinsed pair at the same tag size, but the STF shrinks down. That is why you size up two [3].
- When I ignored the advice and bought a 29 waist, I could barely pull them on and couldn't breathe [4].
- The waist did stretch out over the following week, though [5].
- Before you soak them they'll feel too big, but they fit normally once wet [6].

**Why two inches more in length**
- In my own pair the length barely shrank, and I would have gotten a 32 [7].

**Sizes I haven't covered**
- I haven't said whether a 35 waist is actually made. I only noted that a 36 might not exist when sizing up from a 34 [1].

questions.question: Why do you cuff your jeans?

hybrid.answer:
I cuff mainly because I can't settle on a hem length. Cuffing is the only fix I've found for that, apart from committing to one fit [1].

**Hem length:** I can never decide between no break, half break or full break, so I end up thinking each pair I buy is the wrong length. Cuffing lets me adjust [1].

**Style:** On my Levi's 501s, I cuffed them because my current style doesn't suit wider-legged pants left uncuffed. I'd also have bought a 32 length [2].

**Too long looks bad:** For me, length is the most important thing. If jeans look too long they just look bad, and the cuff shouldn't be too thick [3].

**Over boots instead:** I used to always cuff, but I now like wearing my jeans down over my boots more [4].

questions.question: So do you prefer [the Red Wing 3335s] over the 1907s?

hybrid.answer:
I've leaned toward the 3335s, but my latest view is more hedged. I've said the 3335s are my favorite Red Wings of all time, and they still might be, but probably not [1]. The 1907s, 875s and Iron Rangers each have characteristics I really like [1]. I'm also getting rid of my 3335s [1].

**Why I liked the 3335s**
- They're stitch-down, lighter, more nimble, and easier for walking or a light hike [1].
- They have a Vibram mini lug sole that I don't think will break down as fast as the crepe soles on the 875s and 1907s [2].
- I called them my favorite boots I've ever had, ahead of the 1907s and 875s, and a dramatically better all-around boot for hiking and walking in the woods [3].

**Where the 1907s win**
- The 1907s and 875s are more beefily built, so if you need a tough boot, the 3335s are probably not the ones to go for [3].
- Earlier, I said that if you're looking at a moc toe Red Wing, I think you should get the 1907s [4]. I called them Red Wing's best heritage boots by far, and the storm welt is a big reason [4].

**Overall:** I preferred the 3335s for hiking and all-around wear. I'm no longer sure they're my favorite, and the 1907s are the better pick if you want a tougher heritage boot.

questions.question: How do you feel bout blunnies as of Late 2023?

hybrid.answer:
I'm a big fan of Blundstones and have always loved them [1]. By then I was retiring my worn-in 585s, but that was a cull of my collection, not a change of heart about the boot [1].

**The 585s:** I've worn them constantly. The leather is beat up and shiny, but they've held up through it all [1]. They've stayed probably my most water resistant boots [1]. I also note that some people really don't like Blundstones [1].

**Slip-on use:** I like Blundstones as shoes I can flop on quickly for errands or in the rain [2]. I was keeping that kind of pair, though I said it could easily go on the sell list [2].

**The heavy-duty work boots:** I thought they were waterproof, but they're only a very water resistant nubuck [3].

**Where I started:** In my first video on them, I recommended them 100% as long as you're going to treat them [4]. Without treatment, I'd get plastic or Gore-Tex boots instead [4]. I called them by far my favorites out of the three or four boots I had then [5].

hybrid.answer:
**Short answer:** I'm retiring my Blundstone 585s, the pair from my first video, as part of cutting down my boot collection. They held up well to the end [1].

**Where they stand now:** They've been worn constantly and the leather is beat up and shiny, with old wax conditioner on it [1]. They've held up through all of that and stayed probably my most water resistant boots [1]. I'm a big fan of Blundstones and have always loved them [1].

questions.question: How does the made in England boot stack up to Solovairs? [Dr. Martens]

hybrid.answer:
I think Solovair is the better boot, and it's cheaper. I still like my Solovairs after a quality-control problem. I'd only sell them to buy another pair of monkey boots, and the only reason is that the fit is loose [1]. In the direct comparison, my answer is that Solovair is better and Doc Martens is worse [2].

**Where Solovair wins**
- **Midsole:** Both have felted midsoles, but Solovair's are thicker, heavier and more robust. That gives more padding and insulation, and they take longer to crush down [3].
- **Leather:** Solovair does use full grain leather. Check the specific model before buying, though, because some Solovairs aren't full grain and some Doc Martens are [4][5].
- **Comfort:** Solovairs have a shank, which makes them more comfortable over long periods. Doc Martens don't have one [6].
- **Repairs:** Solovair sells its soles on its website, so you can repair them yourself or have them do it. That's why I think they have a much longer lifespan than Docs [7].
- **Price:** Solovairs are $40 cheaper. I see that as a better boot at a lower price, without Doc Martens' markup [8].

**Where Made in England Docs hold up**
- The leather is better and should age fine, probably on par with Solovair. The midsoles are probably on par too [9].
- Solovair can't do the yellow stitching. If that matters to you, you'll want the Made in England Docs for the highest quality [10].
- For a Doc Martens fan, the England boots make sense. On pure value, are they worth the extra $90? Probably not [11]. You have to be a mega fan to get them [12].

**Solovair downsides**
- My Solovair laces ripped, and I suspect the rough inside of the eyelets could do it again. That's my only gripe [13].
- The pair I got was really big, so size down and check the comments on sizing [14].

questions.question: Hi, I am going on a 4 day hike and I am wondering if I can use my blundstone for them, what do you think?

hybrid.answer:
I haven't covered multi-day hiking in Blundstones, so I can't give you a direct verdict for a 4-day trip. From what I have said, I wouldn't call them a great hiking boot.

**Support:** I took mine up and down a few mountains in Maine, and they held up well, but they aren't good boots for mountain hiking because they don't have good ankle support [1]. I got them a little scuffed up on the way [1].

**Comfort and break-in:** I got big break-in blisters once I started running and walking a track in them, and it took about two to three weeks before they stopped [2]. If you go, make sure yours are properly broken in first.

**Water:** After a year untreated, they were fine for crossing a brook or stream or standing in some mud [3]. Keep the leather treated, because that's what keeps them water resistant [4].

**Compared with other boots:** For hikes and walking in the woods, I like my Red Wing 3335s better than my Blundstones [5]. I'd consider them for a shorter walk, but for four days I'd lean toward something with more ankle support.

questions.question: I'm 5'11-225 lbs with a dad bod. What's the most cost efficient and quality t shirt for me? Also, what size would u prefer?

hybrid.answer:
**My pick for you is Muji.** Uniqlo at $20 is the best t-shirt for the price, but if you're taller or wider you'd want Muji [1]. It costs $4 or $5 more, but it's significantly longer and a good deal wider, so you'd probably like it if you're a little bigger [2]. In an earlier comparison I also said Muji's shirt feels better than Uniqlo's and that the extra cost feels justified [3].

**Other value options:**
- **Front General Store:** a $40 shirt made entirely in Japan, with great proportions and feel. It's my pick for best value among the cheaper shirts right now [4][5].
- **House of Blanks:** $35, made in Canada, with no torquing at all. I called it an outstanding value [6].
- **Los Angeles Apparel:** it runs very large, but sized down one it might win [7][8].

**Size:** I haven't covered what size to pick for 5'11" and 225 lbs. The closest thing is my own preference for a lot of space across the shoulders [9]. Beyond that, the longer and wider Muji is the one I'd point you to, so I can't name a specific size for you.

questions.question: Where's Whitesville?? It's literally the most well known White Tee from Japan

hybrid.answer:
Whitesville is in my videos: I covered it in both the sweatshirt ranking and the t-shirt ranking, and I rate it well in both.

**Sweatshirt**
- I count it among the best sweatshirts on that list. It's a fantastic quality loopwheel sweatshirt from Japan [1].
- It's very loose and very soft, in a fluffy, cozy way rather than a silky one [2].
- It uses a 5x1 rib knit on the cuffs, hem and collar. You either like that or you don't, and it's not my favorite. I'd prefer a 2x1 or 1x1 [3].
- I spotted a messed-up thread and stitch at the cuff [4].
- It's pre-washed, so it had zero shrinkage [5].
- If you like the 5x1 rib cuff, I'd pick Whitesville over Buzz Rickson's, which comes from the same parent company [6].

**T-shirt**
- It's a Japanese riff on old Americana underwear, cut tight like vintage tees so it wouldn't get in the way of a shirt worn over it [7].
- It's one of the softest tees on the list, and it feels great for the price [8].
- The collar has binding tape, so it holds its shape better over time [9].
- In my shrink test it lost 5.4% in width and 3% in length [10].
- In my superlatives it won the award for the softest, coziest tee [11].

questions.question: Am I the only one who loves these videos but in the end still has no idea which to buy? Please just tell me: buy this one, or these 3. I can't decide between 25 options. [t-shirts]

hybrid.answer:
I don't name one best t-shirt, so I can't honestly say "buy this one." The best t-shirt is whichever one lines up with your preferences [1]. I can narrow it down with what I'd wear most, though.

**My picks by category (latest roundup)**
- **All-arounder:** J Press x American Trench. I like its rougher hand feel [2].
- **Japanese-made:** Wonder Looper, mainly for its more universal fit [3].
- **Heavyweight:** American Giant, because it's a little lighter and fits more universally [4].
- **Premium minimalist:** Merz b. Schwanen. Lady White could be my favorite too, but today I lean toward the MSB [5].
- **Value:** Front General Store if you like character, House of Blanks if you want perfectly smooth with no torque. Today I'm feeling the Front General Store, and tomorrow I might feel House of Blanks [6].

**If you want a shortcut:** for the lowest price, a $20 Uniqlo is probably the best t-shirt you can get for the money [7]. In an earlier ranking, the overall winner I paid for was Asket [8].

If you want three, pick one each from the all-arounder, premium and value groups: J Press x American Trench, Merz b. Schwanen and Front General Store. That's my own narrowing of those winners, not a ranking I made. Start with one and see what fit and hand feel you like.

questions.question: Hi, what are some fall/winter sneakers you'd recommend?

hybrid.answer:
The one I'd point you to for fall and winter is the Samara, the all-weather sneaker I made with Goral. It's my favorite hiking shoe [1].

- **Water resistance:** The upper uses a leather that is highly water resistant and doesn't stretch during lasting [2].
- **Cold-weather outsole:** The Vibram Arctic Grip outsole is meant to increase slip resistance on wet ice [3]. It also has a lug that turns blue below freezing to warn you about ice [3].
- **Disclosure:** This is a collaboration with my own brand, so it's my own product.

Two other sneakers I like, though I haven't tied either to cold weather:

- **New Balance 990 V6:** I highly recommend it as a lifestyle and walking shoe [4].
- **Feit Classic Lows:** I wear them every day and they're my favorite sneakers [5].

I haven't said which sneakers are best for cold or wet conditions beyond the Samara.

questions.question: 1907 vs the 875's? What's the difference?

hybrid.answer:
I'd go for the 1907s if you're choosing between the two moc toes. The 1907 is a Goodyear-welted boot with a storm welt, a removable leather footbed and leather laces, for about $10 more than the 875 [1][2].

**Where I stand now:** I've since called the Red Wing 3335 my favorite Red Wing, and it might still be. I still say the 875, the 1907 and the Iron Ranger each have characteristics I really like [3]. I also recommend the 1907s [4].

**Construction and welt:**
- The 875 is Goodyear welted. Goodyear welts are durable and pretty water resistant, and the space inside the welt can hold cork that molds to your foot [5].
- The 1907 adds a storm welt. From what I've seen on Reddit, Red Wing's version is basically another strip of leather stitched onto the welt, not a true Norwegian welt [6]. I'm not sure exactly how it works.

**Price and what you get:**
- The 1907 costs about $10 more than the 875, but I argue that's not a real difference [7].
- The extra money gets you Red Wing's leather footbed, which you can usually buy separately for $40, and it also helps the boots dry faster [8].
- You also get leather laces thrown in [8].

**What they share:**
- Both have crepe soles, which I expect to break down faster than the Vibram sole on the 3335 [9].
- Both are more beefily built than the 3335, so they're the ones to pick if you need a tough boot [10].

**Water:**
- In my standing-in-water test of the 1907s, the right boot leaked almost immediately and the left stayed dry. I'd still expect them to hold up fine in rain, grass or mud [11].
- I haven't tested the 875s the same way, so I can't compare them on water.

questions.question: How does Uniqlo compare to The Front General Store,  Proclub, and Hanes? ie what is the best budget shirt?

hybrid.answer:
**Uniqlo is my pick for the best budget t-shirt, with the Front General Store as the step up if you can spend about twice as much.** For the price, the $20 Uniqlo is probably the best t-shirt you can get [1]. I haven't compared Uniqlo directly against Hanes or Pro Club in a side-by-side, so what follows is how I rated each one.

**Uniqlo**
- It's open-end and a bit rough, and I think of it as the starter t-shirt [2].
- The bound neck collar keeps it from wiggling, and the price-to-quality ratio is insane [3].
- If you're taller or wider, I'd point you to Muji instead [2].
- A couple of shirts rank slightly above it on value: Bravestar and Bronson are neck and neck for the greatest value [4].

**The Front General Store**
- It's a $40 shirt made 100% in Japan, with great proportions and a great feel [5].
- It's one of the best shirts you can get if you want an upgrade without spending over $40 [6]. I rated its softness 6 out of 10 [6].
- If you want a lot of character, this is the one, and it's the one I'm feeling on the day I made that call [7].

**Pro Club**
- It's the roughest shirt on the list, but I like everything about it [8].
- I gave it a softness of 4 out of 10 [8].

**Hanes**
- It's a classic $10 great shirt [9] and much softer than Pro Club [10].
- I gave it a softness of 7 out of 10 [9].

**Bottom line:** For the cheapest solid shirt, I'd go Uniqlo. If you want more character and Japanese construction, I'd pay for the Front General Store. Hanes is the softer of the two cheapest options, and Pro Club is the rougher one.

questions.question: Would you recommend this [Barbour Bedale] or the flint and tinder for someone who would use it like a rain jacket but also a windbreaker and a spring light jacket?

hybrid.answer:
**I'd lean toward the Bedale for this**, mainly because of the rain use. I haven't compared the two head to head for rain, wind and spring wear, so that's a lean and not a firm verdict.

**Barbour Bedale**
- It isn't a designated rain jacket, since the fabric is lightweight [1]. It's also comfortable in any season, so it works as a spring jacket too [1].
- With fresh wax it didn't leak at all in my shower test [2]. It isn't waterproof, but it's very water-resistant when properly treated [2].
- The catch is that as the patina develops, you lose a little water resistance [3]. You'd need to keep the wax up.
- Its rain features are what tip it for me: storm cuffs [4], a storm flap over the zipper [5], and a hood that snaps on [6]. I highly suggest buying the hood [6].
- On wind, I found that the thornproof finish adds wind and water resistance because the weave is tighter [7]. I haven't tied that to the Bedale specifically.

**Flint and Tinder Waxed Trucker**
- I called it a jacket for everyone, in a segment sponsored by Huckberry. I said I had praised it many times before the sponsorship [8].
- It's lighter weight but not crazy lightweight, and it's comfortable [8]. The canvas is 7 oz and very lightweight, and it ages quickly because of its high wax content [9].
- In an earlier video, though, I said it's for a specific man who isn't me [10].
- I haven't tested its rain or wind performance, and I haven't covered its rain features, so I can't say how it compares on those.

questions.question: Great video. But just curious, how can you say it's a con that the Huckberry jacket is unlined when they sell two different versions of lined waxed truckers: wool, and flannel?

hybrid.answer:
The con applies only to the unlined version I showed in that video, and I know the lined versions exist. I forgot to record that part in the video and added it afterward: the Huckberry and Rogue Territory jackets I showed are unlined. I always like a liner on a waxed jacket so the wax doesn't touch your clothes or arms [1].

**The lined versions.** The jacket I reviewed first was lined, and I noted that Huckberry also offers one without a lining [2]. Since then I've said the lined Flint and Tinder trucker is comfortable and keeps wax off your skin [3]. The wool-lined one is a nicer, heavier version that I haven't tried yet [3]. I've also said the wool-lined version is made in much more limited quantities, so you have to sign up for notifications [4].

**My view on lining has softened.** I used to want a liner on almost every waxed jacket because the wax gets on your skin [5]. Now I see why you might leave a jacket unlined. A satin sleeve lining can stick to your skin once it's a bit warm, which limits how often you can wear the jacket [6].

So the unlined version is still a con for me, but a smaller one than it used to be. The lined versions are there if you want a liner.
